items.name: Alki Beach Park
items.blurb: Alki is West Seattle's long city beach, looking across Elliott Bay to the downtown skyline. Designated fire rings are set up along the sand for cookouts. Look for the replica of the Statue of Liberty and the obelisk marking the 1851 settlement. A paved beach trail runs along Alki Avenue for walking and cycling.

items.name: Golden Gardens Park
items.blurb: This Ballard park faces west over Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains, making it a favorite for sunsets. Beach fire pits are available, and the tide pools and loop trails give visitors plenty to explore. An off-leash dog area sits at the northern end. The Burke-Gilman Trail ends here, so it is also an easy bike destination.

items.name: Lincoln Park
items.blurb: Lincoln Park in West Seattle pairs a pebbly Puget Sound beach with a big play area. Colman Pool, an Olympic-size heated saltwater pool with a waterslide, is on site. There are five picnic shelters, a playground, cable rides and a tree house for kids.

items.name: Carkeek Park
items.blurb: Carkeek is a 216-acre watershed park in north Seattle with about six miles of forest trails. A pedestrian bridge crosses the railroad tracks to reach a Puget Sound beach, and the sound views are comparable to Alki's. It is a quieter pick if you want woods and water in one outing.

items.name: Matthews Beach Park
items.blurb: On the shore of Lake Washington in northeast Seattle, Matthews Beach has the city's largest sheltered, shallow swim beach. A floating dock, lifeguards in season and changing rooms make it good for families.

items.name: Constellation Park
items.blurb: Just south of Alki, this small West Seattle shoreline is one of the city's most popular tide-pooling spots. Visitors come at low tide to look at sea life in the rocks, and the park is also listed as a place for evening bonfires.

items.name: Magnuson Park
items.blurb: Magnuson Park on Lake Washington has a beachfront, an off-leash dog area and open fields. Its 1930s and 1940s Art Deco and brick buildings recall its past as a naval air station. Sail Sand Point, which rents boats and paddleboards, is nearby.

items.name: Myrtle Edwards Park
items.blurb: A waterfront strip north of Belltown, Myrtle Edwards has a paved bike and walking path along Elliott Bay. It is one of the closest shorelines to downtown and is a good picnic stop next to the Olympic Sculpture Park.

items.name: Pier 62 Waterfront Park
items.blurb: Pier 62 is a rebuilt historic pier on the downtown waterfront, listed by Visit Seattle as the city's newest public waterfront space. It offers art, food and views of ferries crossing Elliott Bay.

items.name: Discovery Park
items.blurb: At 534 acres, Discovery Park in Magnolia is the city's largest park, with meadows, forest, sea cliffs and tidal beaches. It is a former military base, and it holds the Daybreak Star Indian Cultural Center. The renovated play area has a zip line and picnic tables. A steep trail drops to the beach and the West Point Lighthouse.

items.name: Seward Park
items.blurb: Seward Park is a 300-acre peninsula on Lake Washington with one of the city's last stands of old-growth forest. A paved loop of about 2.4 miles suits walkers and cyclists. There is a swimming beach with lifeguards at select times, a boat launch, and the Seward Park Audubon Center for bird tours.

items.name: Green Lake Park
items.blurb: Green Lake is the city's busiest loop for runners, walkers, cyclists and strollers, with a path of roughly three miles. The lake has two swimming beaches, and the Greenlake Boathouse rents paddle craft. It was designed by John Olmsted in 1903 and is quieter on weekdays.
items.address: 7201 E Green Lake Dr N, Seattle

items.name: Gas Works Park
items.blurb: Gas Works sits on the site of a former coal gasification plant, and rusted towers and machinery were left in place as industrial sculpture. The hill above offers views of Lake Union and the downtown skyline and is a favorite spot for kite flying.

items.name: Volunteer Park
items.blurb: This Capitol Hill park of about 48 acres was designed by the Olmsted Brothers. It holds the Volunteer Park Conservatory, a Victorian glasshouse botanical garden, the Seattle Asian Art Museum, and a historic water tower that visitors can climb for a view. The park also has a stage for outdoor performances.

items.name: Washington Park Arboretum
items.blurb: Run by the University of Washington, the Arboretum covers about 230 acres of marked paths lined with azaleas, rhododendrons and Japanese maples. The Seattle Japanese Garden is inside the grounds and is open March to November.

items.name: Kerry Park
items.blurb: Small Queen Anne park known for one of the classic skyline views of Seattle, with the Space Needle, downtown and Elliott Bay in the frame. On a clear day Mount Rainier appears behind. It faces south and can get crowded around sunset.

items.name: Lake Union Park
items.blurb: In South Lake Union, this park sits next to the Museum of History and Industry and the Center for Wooden Boats, which makes it a handy stop for a lakeside stroll. It also has a beach spot known as Goose Beach.

items.name: Woodland Park
items.blurb: Woodland Park near Green Lake offers sports courts, a rose garden and lake views. Woodland Park Zoo is on the same grounds, in Phinney Ridge.

items.name: Oxbow Park
items.blurb: A small Georgetown park best known for a large cowboy hat and boots sculpture. The art began life as a gas station, which operated from the late 1950s to the late 1980s.

items.name: Discovery Park Loop and North Beach Trail
items.blurb: Discovery Park's named trails include the Loop Trail and the Beach Trail. The North Beach Trail passes a dramatic lighthouse, and a steep path leads down to Puget Sound. Allow time for the climb back up.

items.name: Carkeek Park Pipers Creek Trail
items.blurb: The Pipers Creek Trail winds through Carkeek's wooded watershed with Puget Sound views. The park has about six miles of forest trails in all, plus a footbridge to the beach.

items.name: Union Bay Natural Area and Yesler Swamp
items.blurb: Run by the University of Washington Botanic Gardens, this wetland area is known for the Yesler Swamp trail. It is a calm option for bird watching close to the city.
items.address: Center for Urban Horticulture, University of Washington

items.name: Seward Park Sqebeqsed Trail
items.blurb: This trail is popular for bird-watching and for views across Lake Washington. It is one of several walks in Seward Park's old-growth forest.

items.name: Washington Park Arboretum Trails
items.blurb: About 230 acres of marked paths wind past rare plants and seasonal color. The Seattle Japanese Garden within is open March to November.

items.name: Hiram M. Chittenden Locks (Ballard Locks)
items.blurb: The locks regulate water between Puget Sound and the Lake Washington Ship Canal. A visitor center is on site, and a salmon fish ladder can be viewed from May to September. The Carl S. English Jr. Botanical Garden is on the grounds.

items.name: Overlook Walk
items.blurb: An elevated pedestrian route on the waterfront that links Pike Place Market to the Seattle Aquarium.

items.name: Green Lake Loop
items.blurb: The paved loop around Green Lake is roughly three miles and takes about an hour on foot. It is shared with runners and cyclists, so weekdays are calmer.
items.address: 7201 E Green Lake Dr N, Seattle

items.name: Kobe Terrace Park
items.blurb: In the Chinatown-International District, Kobe Terrace has cherry blossoms in spring and a stone lantern said to be 200 years old. It is a short walk from the Wing Luke Museum and the Seattle Pinball Museum.

items.name: Burke-Gilman Trail
items.blurb: Nearly 20 miles of converted railroad bed, running from Golden Gardens Park in Ballard to Kenmore. It is off limits to motorized vehicles except e-bikes, and it links Puget Sound, Lake Union and Lake Washington.

items.name: Elliott Bay Trail
items.blurb: A 3.9-mile route along the downtown waterfront, with public art, history, wildlife and views of mountains and water. It passes through parkland in the center of the city.

items.name: Ship Canal Trail
items.blurb: A 1.9-mile path on the south side of the Lake Washington Ship Canal, facing the Burke-Gilman Trail across the water.
items.address: South side of the Ship Canal, Seattle

items.name: Alki Beach Trail
items.blurb: A flat, serene path of roughly four miles along Alki Avenue and the beach in West Seattle. It is not a loop, so plan on an out-and-back ride.

items.name: Duwamish Trail
items.blurb: A 3-mile north-south trail along the industrial Duwamish Waterway. It is described as an important connector in southwest Seattle.

items.name: Interurban Trail North
items.blurb: At 31.3 miles, this long trail follows the route of the original electric railway between Seattle and Everett through residential and commercial areas.

items.name: Myrtle Edwards Park Path
items.blurb: A bike and walking path along Elliott Bay just north of Belltown. It runs along Elliott Bay just north of Belltown.

items.name: Seattle Bike Web Map
items.blurb: The City of Seattle's online bike map is the place to plan a route. Pair it with local rentals such as Evo Seattle, Montlake Bicycle Shop or Recycled Cycles.

items.name: Bikeshare and E-bike Rentals
items.blurb: For a quick ride, the Visit Seattle guide lists Lime, Bird and Veo for bikeshare e-bikes and scooters.

items.name: West Point Lighthouse
items.blurb: Built in 1881, this lighthouse on the northern tip of Discovery Park is still active. Reach it on the beach trail from the park, with a steep walk back up. It looks out over Puget Sound.
items.address: Discovery Park, 3801 Discovery Park Blvd, Seattle

items.name: Point No Point Lighthouse
items.blurb: Across the Sound on the Kitsap Peninsula, a peaceful beach is anchored by an 1879 lighthouse. It makes a day trip by ferry and car.

items.name: Space Needle
items.blurb: Opened for the 1962 World's Fair, the Space Needle has an observation deck about 520 feet up with 360-degree views of downtown, Elliott Bay, the Olympics and Mount Rainier. A rotating glass floor is a highlight.

items.name: Sky View Observatory
items.blurb: On the 73rd floor of the Columbia Center, Seattle's tallest building, this observation deck looks down on the Space Needle.

items.name: Kerry Park
items.blurb: Queen Anne's classic viewpoint for the skyline, the Space Needle and, on clear days, Mount Rainier. It faces south and gets crowded at sunset.

items.name: Gas Works Park Hill
items.blurb: The hillside at Gas Works is a favorite for views of Lake Union and the downtown skyline, and for kite flying.

items.name: Volunteer Park Water Tower
items.blurb: A historic water tower in Volunteer Park can be climbed for a view over Capitol Hill and beyond.

items.name: Alki Beach Viewpoint
items.blurb: A 2.5-mile beach path in West Seattle gives views of the water and, across Elliott Bay, the Space Needle and skyline.

items.name: Museum of History & Industry (MOHAI)
items.blurb: MOHAI occupies four stories at the south end of Lake Union and covers regional history from the Duwamish peoples to the modern tech industry, including the Great Seattle Fire of 1889. It houses the Bezos Center for Innovation. The Center for Wooden Boats is next door.

items.name: The Museum of Flight
items.blurb: One of the largest air and space museums in the world, with the Great Gallery, the Personal Courage Wing and the original Boeing headquarters. It holds more than 175 aircraft and spacecraft and a tourable Air Force One. It is about eight miles from downtown.

items.name: Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture
items.blurb: The state's oldest public museum, founded in 1885 and now on the University of Washington campus. It holds fossils, Northwest Native art and natural history collections, and a working research lab is visible through large windows. Admission is waived on the first Thursday of each month.

items.name: Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park, Seattle Unit
items.blurb: Part of the national historical park, this Pioneer Square museum tells how Seattle became the outfitting hub of the Klondike gold rush.

items.name: Wing Luke Museum
items.blurb: A museum of Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander history, art and culture in the Chinatown-International District.

items.name: National Nordic Museum
items.blurb: Covers the history of Denmark, Norway, Finland, Sweden and Iceland and their ties to the Pacific Northwest. It holds over 80,000 artifacts, a cafe, and an outdoor garden with a replica Viking ship.

items.name: Seattle Underground Tour
items.blurb: A 75-minute guided walk through abandoned storefronts and sidewalks left when Pioneer Square streets were raised after the Great Seattle Fire. The ground is uneven and dimly lit, so wear sensible shoes.

items.name: Pioneer Square
items.blurb: Seattle's original neighborhood, with Richardson Romanesque buildings from the 19th century, art galleries, cafes and an Occidental Square bocce court. It sits next to Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park.

items.name: Seattle Pinball Museum
items.blurb: In the International District, about 50 playable pinball machines, some dating to the 1930s, rotate through the space. Admission includes unlimited play, and vintage sodas are sold.

items.name: Northwest African American Museum
items.blurb: Housed in the historic Colman School building in the Central District, with exhibits from contemporary art to historical photographs. Jimi Hendrix Park is next door.

items.name: Seattle Art Museum (SAM)
items.blurb: SAM's downtown building holds more than 25,000 works from around the world, including Pacific Northwest Native art and contemporary pieces. It runs the Olympic Sculpture Park and the Seattle Asian Art Museum.

items.name: Olympic Sculpture Park
items.blurb: A waterfront park of about nine acres, part of SAM, with monumental sculpture including works by Alexander Calder and Richard Serra. It offers views of the Space Needle, Puget Sound and the Olympics.

items.name: Chihuly Garden and Glass
items.blurb: Dale Chihuly's glasswork fills eight galleries, an outdoor garden with the Space Needle behind it, and a 40-foot Glasshouse. Glassblowing demonstrations are held daily.

items.name: Frye Art Museum
items.blurb: An intimate collection of 19th-century, modern and contemporary art .

items.name: Seattle Asian Art Museum
items.blurb: SAM's Asian art museum is in Volunteer Park on Capitol Hill.

items.name: Volunteer Park Conservatory
items.blurb: A Victorian glasshouse botanical garden in Volunteer Park. The park's dahlias bloom from July.

items.name: Seattle Japanese Garden
items.blurb: A 3.5-acre garden in the Washington Park Arboretum, open March to November.

items.name: Fremont Troll
items.blurb: An 18-foot sculpture weighing about 6.5 tons that lurks under the George Washington Memorial Bridge in Fremont.

items.name: Wa Na Wari
items.blurb: A community space in the Central District showcasing Black art. It hosts the Walk the Block art festival each September.

items.name: Pacific Science Center
items.blurb: Housed in 1962 World's Fair buildings at Seattle Center, with hands-on science, a tropical butterfly house, a planetarium and the state's largest IMAX screen. Check the website for current hours.

items.name: Seattle Aquarium
items.blurb: On Pier 59 on the waterfront, with more than 10,000 marine animals and a 360,000-gallon tank. Residents include seals, sea otters, tufted puffins and a giant Pacific octopus.

items.name: Woodland Park Zoo
items.blurb: A zoo on Phinney Ridge with habitats from around the world, known for conservation work. The summer ZooTunes concert series is held here.

items.name: Seattle Children's Museum
items.blurb: Interactive exhibits for young children at Seattle Center. Check its website before visiting, as the museum has had temporary closures.

items.name: Artists at Play and International Fountain
items.blurb: A kids' playground at Seattle Center with slides, swings, ropes courses and merry-go-rounds, next to the International Fountain splash pad.

items.name: Seattle Great Wheel and Miners Landing
items.blurb: The 175-foot Great Wheel stands on Pier 57 at Miners Landing, which also has an arcade and a carousel.

items.name: Ye Olde Curiosity Shop
items.blurb: A kitschy curios shop steps from Pier 57 on the waterfront.

items.name: Kraken Community Iceplex
items.blurb: Public skating is offered during lunch breaks, evenings and weekends.

items.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation Discovery Center
items.blurb: Exhibits on the foundation's work on global inequality, at Seattle Center.

items.name: REI Pinnacle Climbing Wall
items.blurb: A 65-foot indoor climbing wall at REI with beginner classes, including kids' classes.

items.name: Washington State Ferries: Seattle to Bainbridge Island
items.blurb: The crossing takes about 35 minutes. For the fall schedule, Sep 20 to Dec 26, 2026, there are 23 weekday departures and 22 weekend departures from each side, from early morning to late evening. Fares are on the WSDOT route page.

items.name: Washington State Ferries: Seattle to Bremerton
items.blurb: The crossing takes about an hour. For Sep 20 to Dec 26, 2026, there are 15 daily sailings each way, roughly every 1 to 2 hours. WSDOT lists service alerts on the route page, so check before you go.

items.name: Argosy Cruises
items.blurb: Harbor cruises on Elliott Bay with skyline and mountain views, plus Ballard Locks tours, whale watching and dining cruises. A pier-front booth sells tickets.

items.name: Puget Sound Express Whale Watching
items.blurb: Whale-watching trips on Puget Sound.

items.name: Clipper Vacations Whale Watching
items.blurb: Another operator for whale-watching adventures out of Seattle.

items.name: Seattle's Tall Ship (Bay Lady)
items.blurb: An 85-foot wind-powered schooner for sails on the water.

items.name: Waterways Cruises
items.blurb: Dinner and brunch cruises on Lake Union and Lake Washington.

items.name: Kenmore Air Seaplane Tours
items.blurb: Seaplane flights from South Lake Union, plus flights to the San Juan Islands.

items.name: Salish Sea Tours
items.blurb: Custom catamaran cruises.

items.name: The Center for Wooden Boats
items.blurb: Rents sailboats and human-powered boats at Lake Union Park, next to MOHAI. Boat borrowing is sometimes offered on weekends by reservation.
items.address: Lake Union Park, 860 Terry Ave N, Seattle

items.name: Northwest Outdoor Center
items.blurb: Kayak and stand-up paddleboard rentals on Lake Union.

items.name: Agua Verde Paddle Club
items.blurb: Kayak and paddleboard rentals on Lake Union.

items.name: Alki Kayak Tours
items.blurb: Kayak rentals and guided paddles on Puget Sound with downtown and Olympic mountain views.

items.name: Ballard Kayak & Paddleboard
items.blurb: Kayak and paddleboard rentals and guided paddles on Puget Sound.

items.name: Seattle Paddle
items.blurb: Boat and paddleboard rentals on Lake Washington near Seward Park.

items.name: Sail Sand Point
items.blurb: Boat and paddleboard rentals, with SUP, Hobie and sailboats, near Magnuson and Matthews Beach.

items.name: Green Lake Boathouse
items.blurb: Paddle craft and watersport rentals on Green Lake.

items.name: UW Waterfront Activities Center
items.blurb: Boat rentals on Union Bay at the University of Washington.

items.name: Electric Boat Company
items.blurb: Covered electric boats that carry up to 10 passengers on Lake Union.

items.name: Pike Place Market
items.blurb: One of the country's longest-running markets, open daily, with more than 500 small businesses. Beecher's cheese, Sweetie's Candy, the Market Magic Shop and the original Starbucks are all here, and farmers sell produce and flowers. It has operated since 1907.

items.name: Post Alley Gum Wall
items.blurb: A wall covered in chewed gum that started with theatergoers and is a quirky Pike Place stop.

items.name: University District Farmers Market
items.blurb: Locally grown produce and street food on University Way NE between 50th and 52nd. Held Saturdays.
items.address: University Way NE between 50th and 52nd St, Seattle

items.name: Fremont Sunday Market
items.blurb: A European-style street market with food trucks, vintage clothing and records, and antiques.

items.name: Wallingford Farmers Market
items.blurb: A neighborhood market in Meridian Park, held Wednesdays May to September.

items.name: Capitol Hill Farmers Market
items.blurb: A neighborhood farmers market listed by Visit Seattle among options with outdoor seating.

items.name: Queen Anne Farmers Market
items.blurb: A neighborhood farmers market on Queen Anne.

items.name: Molly Moon's Homemade Ice Cream
items.blurb: Known for Scout Mint, made with Thin Mint cookies, and Melted Chocolate. The University District shop pairs with Hello Robin for cookie sandwiches.

items.name: Shug's Soda Fountain
items.blurb: A downtown soda fountain with a S'More sundae with house-made marshmallows and hot fudge, and an egg cream.

items.name: Frankie & Jo's
items.blurb: A Capitol Hill shop with vegan-friendly flavors such as Salty Caramel Ash and California Cabin.

items.name: Nutty Squirrel Gelato
items.blurb: Italian-style gelato in Phinney Ridge with pistachio, chocolate stracciatella and seasonal flavors. Any flavor can become a milkshake.

items.name: Beecher's Handmade Cheese
items.blurb: A Pike Place Market cheese maker listed among the market's best-known businesses.

items.name: Sweetie's Candy
items.blurb: A candy shop in Pike Place Market.

items.name: Original Starbucks
items.blurb: The first Starbucks stands in Pike Place Market.

items.name: Milstead & Co.
items.blurb: A cafe named among Seattle's coffee stops.

items.name: Storyville Coffee
items.blurb: A Seattle cafe named among the local coffee stops.

items.name: Seven Coffee Roasters
items.blurb: A Seattle cafe named among the local coffee stops.

items.name: Canlis
items.blurb: A midcentury-style restaurant with attentive service, a seasonal Northwest menu and an unusual view. It is expensive.

items.name: Dick's Drive-In
items.blurb: Inexpensive burgers and fries, a Seattle institution.

items.name: The Walrus and the Carpenter
items.blurb: An oyster bar in a whitewashed space; expect a wait for a seat.

items.name: Sitka & Spruce
items.blurb: Praised for Northwest seasonal cooking and original dishes.

items.name: Ivar's Acres of Clams
items.blurb: Waterfront seafood with outdoor seating; the adjacent takeout fish bar serves clams and chips.

items.name: Spinasse
items.blurb: Piedmontese Italian cooking on Capitol Hill; tajarin with butter and sage is the signature. Sister restaurant Artusi is next door.

items.name: How to Cook a Wolf
items.blurb: Italian and Pacific Northwest dishes on a seasonal menu. There is also a Madison Park location.

items.name: Sushi Kashiba
items.blurb: An omakase chef's counter at Pike Place with 5pm, 7pm and 9pm seatings; the 5pm is walk-in only.

items.name: Shiro's Sushi
items.blurb: Edomae-style sushi in Belltown with set courses; reservations online.

items.name: The Pink Door
items.blurb: Italian food with waterfront views and live entertainment on certain nights. Many tables are held for walk-ins.

items.name: Le Pichet
items.blurb: A very small French bistro near Pike Place; reservations by phone.

items.name: Gainsbourg
items.blurb: A French spot in Greenwood with an open kitchen; no reservations.

items.name: Itsumono
items.blurb: Japanese-inspired gastropub in the International District.

items.name: Rupee Bar
items.blurb: Shareable Sri Lankan and Indian-inspired small plates in Ballard; no reservations.

items.name: Ooink
items.blurb: Ramen with a mala-forward style; spice level is your choice.

items.name: Marination Ma Kai
items.blurb: Hawaiian-style food with picnic tables over Elliott Bay in West Seattle.

items.name: Museum of Pop Culture (MoPOP)
items.blurb: A Frank Gehry-designed museum at Seattle Center covering music, film, games and science fiction. It includes a Jimi Hendrix exhibit and a Nirvana exhibit, and a bronze statue of Chris Cornell stands outside.

items.name: Jimi Hendrix Park
items.blurb: A Central District park honoring Seattle-born Hendrix, beside the Northwest African American Museum. It hosts the city's largest Juneteenth event.

items.name: The Crocodile
items.blurb: A Belltown club that was an early stage for Nirvana, Pearl Jam and Mudhoney.

items.name: Showbox
items.blurb: An Art Deco building known for strong bookings.

items.name: Tractor Tavern
items.blurb: A cozy listening space on Ballard Avenue.

items.name: Sunset Tavern
items.blurb: Another cozy Ballard stage with live bands.

items.name: The Vera Project
items.blurb: An all-ages music venue across from KEXP.

items.name: KEXP 90.3 FM
items.blurb: Seattle's listener-supported radio station, begun in 1972. Its Gathering Space hosts intimate concerts.

items.name: Sub Pop Airport Store
items.blurb: Sells gear from Sub Pop, the label credited with launching the grunge scene.

items.name: Dimitriou's Jazz Alley
items.blurb: A long-standing Seattle jazz venue. The Earshot Jazz Festival runs each fall.

items.name: Washington Hall
items.blurb: A historic dance hall that hosted Duke Ellington, Count Basie and Billie Holiday; restored by Historic Seattle.

items.name: Bop Street Records
items.blurb: A Ballard shop selling vinyl LPs, 45s and 78s since 1974.

items.name: Easy Street Records
items.blurb: West Seattle record store with a cafe and in-store shows.

items.name: Sonic Boom Records
items.blurb: A Ballard shop selling records, CDs and cassettes.

items.name: Jive Time Records
items.blurb: Vintage vinyl in Fremont.

items.name: Ballard
items.blurb: A neighborhood known for maritime heritage and a foodie scene, with record stores, music venues and the Ballard Locks nearby.

items.name: Capitol Hill
items.blurb: Tree-lined streets, century-old mansions and nightlife.

items.name: Pioneer Square
items.blurb: Seattle's original neighborhood with eateries and galleries, next to Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park.

items.name: Fremont and Wallingford
items.blurb: A bohemian, artsy area with quirky local claims to fame and a Sunday market.

items.name: Queen Anne
items.blurb: Lower Queen Anne has bars and Seattle Center; upper Queen Anne has historic homes and quiet parks.

items.name: Belltown
items.blurb: High-rise living with lively nightlife, dining and trendy shopping.

items.name: Chinatown-International District
items.blurb: The center of Seattle's Asian community for over a century.

items.name: West Seattle
items.blurb: Seattle's largest neighborhood with a beach-town feel, consignment shops and bakeries.

items.name: University District
items.blurb: Surrounds the University of Washington with cafes, pubs, theaters and shopping.

items.name: Georgetown and SoDo
items.blurb: Industrial areas turning trendy.

items.name: Central District
items.blurb: Longtime hub of Seattle's Black community and its arts scene.

items.name: Columbia City and Rainier Valley
items.blurb: Among the most diverse zip codes in the country.

items.name: 1 Hotel Seattle
items.blurb: 1 Hotel Seattle is listed by Visit Seattle as a Downtown Seattle hotel. Downtown has views of mountains and waterways and the city's major attractions. Call (206) 264-8111 for rates and availability.

items.name: AC Hotel Seattle Downtown
items.blurb: AC Hotel Seattle Downtown is listed by Visit Seattle as a South Lake Union hotel. South Lake Union is Seattle's tech hub, within reach of Lake Union Park, MOHAI and the streetcar. Call (206) 492-7990 for rates and availability.

items.name: Astra Hotel
items.blurb: Astra Hotel is listed by Visit Seattle as a South Lake Union hotel. South Lake Union is Seattle's tech hub, within reach of Lake Union Park, MOHAI and the streetcar. Call (206) 693-6000 for rates and availability.

items.name: Belltown Inn
items.blurb: Belltown Inn is listed by Visit Seattle as a Belltown hotel. Belltown is known for high-rise living and a lively nightlife and dining scene. Call (206) 529-3700 for rates and availability.

items.name: Best Western Plus Pioneer Square Hotel Downtown
items.blurb: Best Western Plus Pioneer Square Hotel Downtown is listed by Visit Seattle as a Pioneer Square hotel. Pioneer Square is Seattle's original neighborhood, beside Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park. Call (206) 340-1234 for rates and availability.

items.name: citizenM Seattle Pioneer Square
items.blurb: citizenM Seattle Pioneer Square is listed by Visit Seattle as a Pioneer Square hotel. Pioneer Square is Seattle's original neighborhood, beside Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park. Call (206) 886-0560 for rates and availability.

items.name: citizenM Seattle South Lake Union
items.blurb: citizenM Seattle South Lake Union is listed by Visit Seattle as a South Lake Union hotel. South Lake Union is Seattle's tech hub, within reach of Lake Union Park, MOHAI and the streetcar. Call (206) 336-3525 for rates and availability.

items.name: Coast Seattle Downtown Hotel by APA
items.blurb: Coast Seattle Downtown Hotel by APA is listed by Visit Seattle as a Downtown Seattle hotel. Downtown has views of mountains and waterways and the city's major attractions. Call (206) 624-0500 for rates and availability.

items.name: Courtyard by Marriott Seattle Downtown/Lake Union
items.blurb: Courtyard by Marriott Seattle Downtown/Lake Union is listed by Visit Seattle as a South Lake Union hotel. South Lake Union is Seattle's tech hub, within reach of Lake Union Park, MOHAI and the streetcar. Call (206) 213-0100 for rates and availability.

items.name: Courtyard Seattle Downtown/Pioneer Square
items.blurb: Courtyard Seattle Downtown/Pioneer Square is listed by Visit Seattle as a Pioneer Square hotel. Pioneer Square is Seattle's original neighborhood, beside Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park. Call (206) 625-1111 for rates and availability.

items.name: Link Light Rail
items.blurb: Sound Transit's Link runs from Angle Lake to Lynwood with 21 stops, including downtown and SEA Airport. Trains come every 8 to 15 minutes. The fare is a flat $3. The airport ride to downtown takes about 40 minutes.

items.name: King County Metro Buses
items.blurb: Metro buses serve downtown and neighborhoods across King County. The fare is $3, payable by ORCA card, exact cash or Transit GO Ticket. Plan trips with the trip planner or the Metro app.

items.name: Seattle Center Monorail
items.blurb: The monorail connects Westlake Center downtown and Seattle Center in about three minutes, with trains every 10 minutes. A one-way fare is $4.00, and ORCA is accepted. Hours extend in summer and for Climate Pledge Arena events.

items.name: South Lake Union Streetcar
items.blurb: A 1.3-mile line with nine stops. It does not run on Thanksgiving or Christmas Day.

items.name: First Hill Streetcar
items.blurb: A 2.5-mile line with 10 stops. The fare is $2.25, or $4.50 for an all-day pass.

items.name: Washington State Ferries
items.blurb: Ferries link downtown Seattle to Bainbridge Island, about 35 minutes, and Bremerton, about an hour. Both routes load at the Seattle Ferry Terminal.

items.name: SEA Airport Transit
items.blurb: Link light rail is the main way downtown from SEA. Taxis and ride-share pick up on the third floor of the parking garage. Premier Airport Shuttle also serves downtown hotels.

items.name: Bike and Scooter Share
items.blurb: Lime, Bird and Veo offer e-bikes and scooters. Bike rentals include Evo Seattle, Montlake Bicycle Shop and Recycled Cycles.
